title: N C M Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation

paper.title: N C M N ext- C oncept M odeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) , a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running 21 × 21\times faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running 10 × 10\times faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM’s ROUGE-L while being 31 × 31\times faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion language models (DLMs) are the leading non-autoregressive language modeling paradigm [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Their main appeal is their ability to produce many tokens at a time through iterative denoising, which can make generation substantially faster than in autoregressive (AR) models that generate one token at a time. This is becoming increasingly important, as language model inference is one of the dominant computational workloads [ 4 , 5 ] . DLMs are moving from research to practice: open models such as LLaDA [ 6 ] scale to billions of parameters, commercial systems such as Mercury [ 7 ] and DiffusionGemma [ 8 ] serve diffusion models in production, and diffusion drafters like DFlash [ 9 ] accelerate AR models through speculative decoding. Next-token prediction generates one token per step, and masked diffusion (discrete diffusion) refines all L L positions at every step. NCM instead generates discrete codes r k i r_{k}^{i} , the i i -th code of level k k , from coarse to fine in K ≪ L K\ll L steps: each step predicts the ℓ k \ell_{k} codes of one level in parallel, conditioned on the reconstruction z ^ ( k − 1 ) \hat{z}^{(k-1)} of the earlier levels, and after the final level, the cumulative reconstruction is decoded into tokens. The promise of DLMs is parallel sampling: generating a sequence in far fewer sequential steps than it has tokens. In practice however: • (i) Many sampling steps. Diffusion models predict tokens in parallel but still perform successive denoising passes. Reducing these passes can substantially degrade generation quality (Figure 5 ), limiting the speed gains from parallelism. • (ii) Expensive sampling steps. Processing the full sequence at every step limits speedups, and bidirectional attention prevents direct reuse of AR-style KV caching [ 10 , 11 ] . • (iii) Large training budgets. DLM training often involves many passes over the same data. For example, strong diffusion baselines such as DUO and MDLM are trained on OpenWebText for 1 1 M steps, processing over 500 500 B tokens [ 12 , 3 , 13 ] . Prior work reduces the number of sampling steps mainly through few-step samplers and distillation, either by distilling a many-step teacher into a few-step student [ 12 , 14 ] or by learning a direct map between noise levels [ 15 ] . These approaches come at the cost of additional training stages on top of an already expensive model. Few-step sampling also comes at a price: distilled models tend to be less diverse than the models they are distilled from. On standard benchmarks such as OpenWebText [ 16 ] and LM1B [ 17 ] , they reach a lower generative perplexity at the expense of sample diversity, as measured by mean per-sample unigram entropy [ 15 ] . Moreover, these approaches leave the per-step cost unchanged. Block-autoregressive diffusion enables KV caching at the cost of parallelism: tokens within each block can be denoised in parallel, but blocks must be generated sequentially, with each waiting for the previous block to finish [ 18 , 19 ] . We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) , a two-stage language modeling framework. A multiscale residual VQ-VAE [ 20 ] encodes text into K K levels of discrete codes, from short coarse representations to longer fine ones. A transformer generates these levels sequentially, predicting all codes within each level in parallel, following next-scale prediction for images [ 21 , 22 ] . NCM achieves (i) high generation quality and diversity in K ≪ L K\ll L steps without distillation (Figure 5 ); (ii) lower sampling cost by processing short code sequences at early levels (Figure 1 ); and (iii) strong performance with fewer training passes over the data (Figure 7 ). We evaluate NCM models at approximately 100 100 M parameters against discrete-diffusion, flow-based, and hybrid baselines, following standard evaluation protocols [ 3 , 12 ] . Across unconditional generation, conditional generation (translation and summarization), and reasoning tasks (Sudoku), we find: • (i) High quality in few steps. Across three unconditional generation datasets (TinyStories, LM1B, and OpenWebText), NCM matches or outperforms strong diffusion baselines with approximately 4 4 – 11 × 11\times fewer function evaluations (NFE), while maintaining sample entropy close to the data (Figure 5 ). On conditional generation (XSum summarization and WMT14 translation), it uses approximately 6 6 – 16 × 16\times fewer NFE than unguided baselines, achieving the best summarization scores and outperforming all but one non-AR translation baseline (Table 2 ). On Sudoku, NCM outperforms AR and diffusion baselines across difficulty levels while using fewer NFE than any of them (Table 3 ). • (ii) Fast inference and effective test-time scaling. Fewer sampling steps and lower per-step cost from shorter coarse levels yield 10 10 – 31 × 31\times faster generation at comparable or better quality (Figures 1 and 5 ). Using the saved time to generate more candidates and select among them with MBR decoding yields about 7 % 7\% higher ROUGE-L than the strongest summarization baseline within the same sampling-time budget (Figure 6 ). • (iii) Lower training budgets. NCM achieves competitive generation quality with approximately 4 4 – 5 × 5\times fewer training tokens than strong diffusion baselines on LM1B and OpenWebText, including both tokenizer and generator training (Figure 7 ; Appendix C ). We also show preliminary scaling results: increasing NCM ’s model size improves generation quality on LM1B at a fixed training-token budget (Figure 6(a) ). Qualitative probes suggest that coarse levels capture global structure while finer levels add detail (Appendix H , Figures 17 – 19 ). sections.heading: Diffusion & Flow-Based Models for Text Generation.
sections.text: Text generation using Diffusion & Flow-Based Models is an iterative refinement process. Discrete methods operate on token sequences [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] ; continuous methods evolve representations of tokens in an embedding space [ 13 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Distillation/flow-map techniques enable reduction of the number of sampling steps [ 12 , 14 , 15 ] ; however, full-sequence formulations still require processing a length- L L representation in every step. Block-Autoregressive Diffusion allows KV caching through sequential block generation: tokens within a block are generated in parallel; however, each block must be generated after the previous blocks [ 18 , 19 ] . NCM modifies both the representation and the generation schedule. NCM generates a learned hierarchy of discrete codes from coarse to fine, and predicts all codes within each level in parallel. Generation therefore follows a short sequence of levels, with fewer positions processed at the early, coarse levels.

sections.heading: Discrete latent variables and next scale prediction.
sections.text: A number of image generative models use discrete tokenizers [ 20 , 26 , 27 ] . Residual quantization corrects for errors made at previous steps and uses those errors to create a new codebook [ 28 ] which has been adapted to neural audio codecs [ 29 , 30 ] . Next-scale prediction generates such hierarchies coarse to fine, one scale at a time in parallel, for fast, high-quality images [ 21 , 22 ] . NCM extends residual quantization and next-scale prediction to text through a hierarchy of discrete codes that determines the generation order. While latent diffusion models generate continuous representations of text [ 31 , 32 ] , NCM produces successive discrete levels. Adapting this approach to text requires learning useful coarse representations without a natural counterpart to image downsampling. Accurate reconstruction is also important: a single token error can alter meaning, prevent code from running, or invalidate a Sudoku solution.

sections.heading: Hierarchical and concept-level text generation.
sections.text: Several approaches organize language modeling around larger units and learned abstractions. MEGABYTE [ 33 ] combines global modeling of byte patches with local byte prediction, while H-Net [ 34 ] learns dynamic chunks within a multistage hierarchy. Large Concept Models [ 35 ] predict sentence representations. ConceptLM [ 36 ] predicts discrete concepts to guide subsequent token generation, and Dynamic Large Concept Models [ 37 ] learn variable-length concepts for computation in a compressed representation space. HDLM [ 38 ] progressively refines tokens through a hierarchy of semantic vocabularies. NCM represents an entire sequence through discrete levels of increasing resolution and generates these levels in order using a shared transformer. Predicting all codes within each level in parallel gives a short generation path, while the shorter coarse levels reduce computation during early steps.

sections.heading: 3 Next-Concept Modeling
sections.text: NCM generates text through a learned coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes. We first train a multiscale residual VQ tokenizer to represent text at progressively finer levels of detail, then freeze it and train a transformer to generate the hierarchy. At each level, the transformer predicts all codes in parallel, conditioned on the cumulative reconstruction of earlier levels. The tokenizer’s decoder maps the completed reconstruction back to text. sections.heading: Conditional generation.
sections.text: NCM supports prompt-conditioned generation through a prefix-LM attention pattern. Prompt tokens are embedded using the frozen VQ-VAE encoder’s token embedding table and projected into the hidden space. Prompt positions attend to each other; each target block attends to the prompt and itself, while prompt positions cannot attend to target blocks.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate NCM along four axes: • Quality. We first assess tokenizer quality through reconstruction accuracy and codebook utilization (§ 4.1 ). We then evaluate unconditional generation on TinyStories [ 40 ] , One Billion Word (LM1B) [ 17 ] , and OpenWebText (OWT) [ 16 ] , measuring generative perplexity alongside sample diversity (§ 4.2 ). For conditional generation, we evaluate WMT14 German–English translation [ 41 ] using BLEU [ 42 , 43 ] and XSum summarization [ 44 ] using ROUGE-1/2/L [ 45 ] (§ 4.3 ). • Efficiency. We compare the number of function evaluations (NFE) and wall-clock time required to achieve a given generation quality, as well as the training-token budgets used to obtain these results (§ 4.6 ). • Reasoning. We compare NCM with autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku, where successful generation requires satisfying interdependent constraints across the entire output (§ 4.4 ). • Scaling. We investigate how scaling the model size improves generation quality and whether NCM ’s fast sampling can translate into further quality gains through additional test-time compute (§ 4.5 ). Across these evaluations, NCM achieves competitive generation quality with substantially lower sampling cost. We train a separate tokenizer and generator for each dataset. Unless otherwise stated, our generators have approximately 100 100 M parameters, comparable to or smaller than the baselines. We follow established evaluation protocols from prior diffusion language modeling work where possible. Appendices B – E provide dataset, architecture, training, and baseline details, along with additional results.

For a fair comparison, NCM is compared against baselines with sample diversity close to that of the ground-truth data. We evaluate NCM on Sudoku, a reasoning task in which every cell of the solution must satisfy the row, column, and box constraints at once. Following the setup of S-FLM [ 50 ] , we report the percentage of completely solved boards at three difficulty levels defined by the number of provided clues ( 40 40 , 35 35 , and 30 30 for easy, medium, and hard, respectively). NCM outperforms both the AR baselines and the strongest diffusion baseline, FMLM+ [ 49 ] , across all three levels of difficulty while using fewer NFE (Table 3 ). NCM ’s coarse-to-fine generation is well suited to tasks that require global planning: NCM refines a representation of the entire board across levels, allowing later levels to correct earlier partial solutions. In contrast, the AR baselines struggle with left-to-right generation, which commits to individual tokens without revising earlier decisions. sections.heading: 4.5 Scaling
sections.text: We study how NCM benefits from additional compute through larger models and increased inference budgets. We evaluate model scaling by increasing generator size and test-time scaling by selecting among multiple candidates using minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding.

sections.heading: Model Scaling.
sections.text: Scaling NCM ’s model size improves both generation quality and sample diversity at a fixed training-token budget (Figure 6(a) ). We train generators with 97M, 317M, and 725M parameters on LM1B, all sharing the same frozen tokenizer. These results suggest that NCM scales effectively, with potential for further gains from larger generators.

sections.heading: Test-Time Scaling.
sections.text: In Figure 1 and Table 2 , we show that NCM matches or outperforms diffusion baselines while using significantly fewer function evaluations (NFEs) and less wall-clock time. A natural question is whether we can convert these efficiency gains into further improvements in quality. We generate multiple candidates and use minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding [ 51 ] to select the candidate with the highest average similarity to the others. sections.heading: Inference Efficiency.
sections.text: In Figure 5 , we show that NCM achieves lower or comparable generative perplexity than the strongest diffusion baselines using far fewer function evaluations (NFE). However, NFE alone does not capture the full inference efficiency picture, since the cost per step differs across different diffusion language models; many DLMs process the full sequence at every step and use samplers that can introduce additional overhead. NCM , on the other hand, processes very few tokens at the coarse levels of its hierarchy, saving compute at these early steps. We benchmark end-to-end wall-clock time for generating 1,024 1{,}024 sequences at batch size 16 16 on a single NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB GPU (Figure 1 ). On LM1B, NCM uses 11 × 11\times fewer NFE than the strongest diffusion language model baseline, DUO, and runs 21 × 21\times faster at better generative perplexity. On XSum, it uses 16 × 16\times fewer NFE than the strongest diffusion baseline, AURORA-LM, and runs 31 × 31\times faster at comparable ROUGE. The speedup gains come from both fewer NFE and a lower average cost per step compared to the DLM baselines. Lower Training Budgets. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce N ext- C oncept M odeling ( NCM ), a two-stage framework that first learns a discrete coarse-to-fine representation of text and then trains a transformer to generate its levels in order. Predicting all codes within each level in parallel provides a short sequential generation path. On unconditional generation across TinyStories, LM1B, and OpenWebText, NCM achieves competitive or better Gen. PPL than strong diffusion baselines with approximately 4 4 – 11 × 11\times fewer function evaluations (NFE), while maintaining sample entropy close to the data. Generation is 10 10 – 21 × 21\times faster on LM1B and OpenWebText. On conditional generation, NCM uses approximately 6 6 – 16 × 16\times fewer NFE than unguided diffusion baselines on WMT14 translation and XSum summarization, achieving competitive translation quality and the best summarization scores. On XSum, it runs 31 × 31\times faster than the strongest diffusion baseline. It also uses approximately 4 4 – 5 × 5\times fewer training tokens than strong diffusion baselines on LM1B and OpenWebText, including both tokenizer and generator training. Finally, preliminary scaling results on LM1B show that increasing the generator size improves generation quality at a fixed training-token budget.

sections.heading: Appendix A Probabilistic Formulation and ELBO
sections.text: We formulate NCM as a hierarchical latent-variable model and derive an evidence lower bound (ELBO) on its text log-likelihood. We consider unconditional generation with deterministic nearest-neighbor code assignments.

(15) This distribution has zero entropy. Its ELBO therefore reduces to the log joint probability of the tokenizer’s assigned hierarchy: ℒ ELBO ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x) ≡ 𝔼 q ( r 1 : K ∣ x ) [ log p θ , ψ ( x , r 1 : K ) − log q ( r 1 : K ∣ x ) ] \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{E}_{q(r_{1:K}\mid x)}\left[\log p_{\theta,\psi}(x,r_{1:K})-\log q(r_{1:K}\mid x)\right] (16) = log p ψ ( x ∣ r ∗ 1 : K ) + log p θ ( r ∗ 1 : K ) \displaystyle=\log p_{\psi}(x\mid r^{*}_{1:K})+\log p_{\theta}(r^{*}_{1:K}) ≤ log ∑ r 1 : K p ψ ( x ∣ r 1 : K ) p θ ( r 1 : K ) = log p θ , ψ ( x ) . \displaystyle\leq\log\sum_{r_{1:K}}p_{\psi}(x\mid r_{1:K})p_{\theta}(r_{1:K})=\log p_{\theta,\psi}(x). The inequality follows because the marginal likelihood sums nonnegative terms and includes the term for r ∗ 1 : K r^{*}_{1:K} . Writing z ^ ∗ ( k ) = z ^ ( k ) ( r 1 : k ∗ ) \hat{z}_{*}^{(k)}=\hat{z}^{(k)}(r^{*}_{1:k}) and substituting ( 12 ) and ( 13 ) gives ℒ ELBO ​ ( x ) = ∑ n = 1 L log ⁡ p ψ ​ ( x n ∣ z ^ ∗ ( K ) ) ⏟ reconstruction + ∑ k = 1 K ∑ i = 1 ℓ k log ⁡ p θ ​ ( r k ∗ i ∣ z ^ ∗ ( k − 1 ) ) ⏟ generation \boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)=\underbrace{\sum_{n=1}^{L}\log p_{\psi}\bigl(x^{n}\mid\hat{z}_{*}^{(K)}\bigr)}_{\text{reconstruction}}+\underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell_{k}}\log p_{\theta}\bigl(r_{k}^{*i}\mid\hat{z}_{*}^{(k-1)}\bigr)}_{\text{generation}}} (17) where r k ∗ i r_{k}^{*i} is the i i th code at level k k in the assigned hierarchy. The gap to the log-likelihood is exactly log ⁡ p θ , ψ ​ ( x ) − ℒ ELBO ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\log p_{\theta,\psi}(x)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x) = D KL ( q ( r 1 : K ∣ x ) ∥ p θ , ψ ( r 1 : K ∣ x ) ) \displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q(r_{1:K}\mid x)\,\|\,p_{\theta,\psi}(r_{1:K}\mid x)\right) (18) = − log p θ , ψ ( r ∗ 1 : K ∣ x ) ≥ 0 . \displaystyle=-\log p_{\theta,\psi}(r^{*}_{1:K}\mid x)\geq 0. Thus, the bound is tight if and only if the posterior assigns probability one to the tokenizer’s hierarchy. With finite softmax logits, the prior and decoder assign positive probability to every hierarchy and text sequence, so the bound and gap are finite. For a frozen tokenizer and decoder, only the generation term depends on θ \theta . With clean conditioning and α = 0 \alpha=0 , the generator loss in Section 3.4 is the negative generation term divided by the total number of codes N = ∑ k = 1 K ℓ k N=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\ell_{k} ; minimizing it therefore maximizes this ELBO over θ \theta . Conditioning corruption and nonuniform level weighting modify that objective. The bound uses the complete hierarchy; nested dropout and the quantization losses used to train the tokenizer are not included in it.

sections.heading: F.3 Code Corruption
sections.text: Figure 13 : Effect of code corruption. Gen. PPL after 10 10 k steps vs. mean corruption rate. Nonzero rates use a shifted linear decreasing schedule; H H is entropy. During training, NCM uses teacher forcing and conditions on clean input codes; during inference, it conditions on its own generated codes. This difference creates opportunities for errors to accumulate across levels. Since codes within each level are generated in parallel, multiple errors can enter the reconstruction used to generate the next level. We address this mismatch by making the model resilient to incorrect input codes: during training, we replace some input codes with entries sampled uniformly from the same level’s codebook, at a different rate per level. Targets remain clean. This ablation and the loss-weighting ablation (Appendix F.2.3 ) use TinyStories ( 128 128 tokens) and the 12 12 -level tokenizer of Table 5 . Each 88.6 88.6 M NCM transformer is trained for 10,000 10{,}000 steps with a batch size of 1,024 1{,}024 . Gen. PPL is averaged over five sampling seeds with 256 256 samples each. The degree of corruption matters: moderate corruption greatly improves generation quality, while excessive corruption weakens the conditioning signal and degrades quality (Figure 13 ). The type of corruption, including how rates vary across levels and which replacement codes are selected, also affects how closely training resembles generation. We use a linearly decreasing corruption rate across levels. Corruption based on the model’s actual errors may better match inference conditions; we leave this to future work.

sections.heading: Appendix I Limitations & Future Work
sections.text: NCM shows promising results on unconditional generation and downstream conditional generation tasks such as summarization and translation. Several directions remain for further improvement. NCM fixes both the hierarchy depth K K and the per-level lengths ℓ k \ell_{k} , so even short continuations traverse the full hierarchy; an input-dependent schedule would adapt compute to example complexity. NCM relies on a separately trained multiscale VQ-VAE tokenizer, decoupling representation learning from the generative objective. An end-to-end training approach could benefit NCM by aligning representation learning with the generative objective. Our main experiments use generators of roughly 100 100 M parameters, and our scaling study extends to 725 725 M parameters on LM1B. Scaling to larger datasets and model sizes is another exciting direction. Generations are generally fluent but exhibit occasional artifacts at coarse-level transitions, presenting another opportunity to further improve NCM .

Their main appeal is their ability to produce many tokens at a time through iterative denoising, which can make generation substantially faster than in autoregressive (AR) models that generate one token at a time. This is becoming increasingly important, as language model inference is one of the dominant computational workloads [ 4 , 5 ] . DLMs are moving from research to practice: open models such as LLaDA [ 6 ] scale to billions of parameters, commercial systems such as Mercury [ 7 ] and DiffusionGemma [ 8 ] serve diffusion models in production, and diffusion drafters like DFlash [ 9 ] accelerate AR models through speculative decoding. The promise of DLMs is parallel sampling: generating a sequence in far fewer sequential steps than it has tokens. In practice however: • (i) Many sampling steps. Diffusion models predict tokens in parallel but still perform successive denoising passes. Reducing these passes can substantially degrade generation quality (Figure 5 ), limiting the speed gains from parallelism. • (ii) Expensive sampling steps. Processing the full sequence at every step limits speedups, and bidirectional attention prevents direct reuse of AR-style KV caching [ 10 , 11 ] . • (iii) Large training budgets. DLM training often involves many passes over the same data. For example, strong diffusion baselines such as DUO and MDLM are trained on OpenWebText for 1 1 M steps, processing over 500 500 B tokens [ 12 , 3 , 13 ] . Prior work reduces the number of sampling steps mainly through few-step samplers and distillation, either by distilling a many-step teacher into a few-step student [ 12 , 14 ] or by learning a direct map between noise levels [ 15 ] . These approaches come at the cost of additional training stages on top of an already expensive model. Few-step sampling also comes at a price: distilled models tend to be less diverse than the models they are distilled from. On standard benchmarks such as OpenWebText [ 16 ] and LM1B [ 17 ] , they reach a lower generative perplexity at the expense of sample diversity, as measured by mean per-sample unigram entropy [ 15 ] . Moreover, these approaches leave the per-step cost unchanged. Block-autoregressive diffusion enables KV caching at the cost of parallelism: tokens within each block can be denoised in parallel, but blocks must be generated sequentially, with each waiting for the previous block to finish [ 18 , 19 ] . We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM) , a two-stage language modeling framework. A multiscale residual VQ-VAE [ 20 ] encodes text into K K levels of discrete codes, from short coarse representations to longer fine ones. A transformer generates these levels sequentially, predicting all codes within each level in parallel, following next-scale prediction for images [ 21 , 22 ] . NCM achieves (i) high generation quality and diversity in K ≪ L K\ll L steps without distillation (Figure 5 ); (ii) lower sampling cost by processing short code sequences at early levels (Figure 1 ); and (iii) strong performance with fewer training passes over the data (Figure 7 ). We evaluate NCM models at approximately 100 100 M parameters against discrete-diffusion, flow-based, and hybrid baselines, following standard evaluation protocols [ 3 , 12 ] . Across unconditional generation, conditional generation (translation and summarization), and reasoning tasks (Sudoku), we find: • (i) High quality in few steps. Across three unconditional generation datasets (TinyStories, LM1B, and OpenWebText), NCM matches or outperforms strong diffusion baselines with approximately 4 4 – 11 × 11\times fewer function evaluations (NFE), while maintaining sample entropy close to the data (Figure 5 ). On conditional generation (XSum summarization and WMT14 translation), it uses approximately 6 6 – 16 × 16\times fewer NFE than unguided baselines, achieving the best summarization scores and outperforming all but one non-AR translation baseline (Table 2 ). On Sudoku, NCM outperforms AR and diffusion baselines across difficulty levels while using fewer NFE than any of them (Table 3 ). • (ii) Fast inference and effective test-time scaling. Fewer sampling steps and lower per-step cost from shorter coarse levels yield 10 10 – 31 × 31\times faster generation at comparable or better quality (Figures 1 and 5 ). Using the saved time to generate more candidates and select among them with MBR decoding yields about 7 % 7\% higher ROUGE-L than the strongest summarization baseline within the same sampling-time budget (Figure 6 ). • (iii) Lower training budgets. NCM achieves competitive generation quality with approximately 4 4 – 5 × 5\times fewer training tokens than strong diffusion baselines on LM1B and OpenWebText, including both tokenizer and generator training (Figure 7 ; Appendix C ). We also show preliminary scaling results: increasing NCM ’s model size improves generation quality on LM1B at a fixed training-token budget (Figure 6(a) ). Qualitative probes suggest that coarse levels capture global structure while finer levels add detail (Appendix H , Figures 17 – 19 ). Text generation using Diffusion & Flow-Based Models is an iterative refinement process. Discrete methods operate on token sequences [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] ; continuous methods evolve representations of tokens in an embedding space [ 13 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Distillation/flow-map techniques enable reduction of the number of sampling steps [ 12 , 14 , 15 ] ; however, full-sequence formulations still require processing a length- L L representation in every step. Block-Autoregressive Diffusion allows KV caching through sequential block generation: tokens within a block are generated in parallel; however, each block must be generated after the previous blocks [ 18 , 19 ] . NCM modifies both the representation and the generation schedule. NCM generates a learned hierarchy of discrete codes from coarse to fine, and predicts all codes within each level in parallel. Generation therefore follows a short sequence of levels, with fewer positions processed at the early, coarse levels. Discrete latent variables and next scale prediction. A number of image generative models use discrete tokenizers [ 20 , 26 , 27 ] . Residual quantization corrects for errors made at previous steps and uses those errors to create a new codebook [ 28 ] which has been adapted to neural audio codecs [ 29 , 30 ] . Next-scale prediction generates such hierarchies coarse to fine, one scale at a time in parallel, for fast, high-quality images [ 21 , 22 ] . NCM extends residual quantization and next-scale prediction to text through a hierarchy of discrete codes that determines the generation order. While latent diffusion models generate continuous representations of text [ 31 , 32 ] , NCM produces successive discrete levels. Adapting this approach to text requires learning useful coarse representations without a natural counterpart to image downsampling. Accurate reconstruction is also important: a single token error can alter meaning, prevent code from running, or invalidate a Sudoku solution. Hierarchical and concept-level text generation. Several approaches organize language modeling around larger units and learned abstractions. MEGABYTE [ 33 ] combines global modeling of byte patches with local byte prediction, while H-Net [ 34 ] learns dynamic chunks within a multistage hierarchy. Large Concept Models [ 35 ] predict sentence representations. ConceptLM [ 36 ] predicts discrete concepts to guide subsequent token generation, and Dynamic Large Concept Models [ 37 ] learn variable-length concepts for computation in a compressed representation space. HDLM [ 38 ] progressively refines tokens through a hierarchy of semantic vocabularies. NCM represents an entire sequence through discrete levels of increasing resolution and generates these levels in order using a shared transformer. Predicting all codes within each level in parallel gives a short generation path, while the shorter coarse levels reduce computation during early steps. 3 Next-Concept Modeling NCM generates text through a learned coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes. We first train a multiscale residual VQ tokenizer to represent text at progressively finer levels of detail, then freeze it and train a transformer to generate the hierarchy. At each level, the transformer predicts all codes in parallel, conditioned on the cumulative reconstruction of earlier levels. The tokenizer’s decoder maps the completed reconstruction back to text. Prompt positions attend to each other; each target block attends to the prompt and itself, while prompt positions cannot attend to target blocks. 4 Experiments We evaluate NCM along four axes: • Quality. We first assess tokenizer quality through reconstruction accuracy and codebook utilization (§ 4.1 ). We then evaluate unconditional generation on TinyStories [ 40 ] , One Billion Word (LM1B) [ 17 ] , and OpenWebText (OWT) [ 16 ] , measuring generative perplexity alongside sample diversity (§ 4.2 ). For conditional generation, we evaluate WMT14 German–English translation [ 41 ] using BLEU [ 42 , 43 ] and XSum summarization [ 44 ] using ROUGE-1/2/L [ 45 ] (§ 4.3 ). • Efficiency. We compare the number of function evaluations (NFE) and wall-clock time required to achieve a given generation quality, as well as the training-token budgets used to obtain these results (§ 4.6 ). • Reasoning. We compare NCM with autoregressive and diffusion baselines on Sudoku, where successful generation requires satisfying interdependent constraints across the entire output (§ 4.4 ). • Scaling. We investigate how scaling the model size improves generation quality and whether NCM ’s fast sampling can translate into further quality gains through additional test-time compute (§ 4.5 ). Across these evaluations, NCM achieves competitive generation quality with substantially lower sampling cost. We train a separate tokenizer and generator for each dataset. Unless otherwise stated, our generators have approximately 100 100 M parameters, comparable to or smaller than the baselines. We follow established evaluation protocols from prior diffusion language modeling work where possible. In Figure 5 , we show that NCM achieves lower or comparable generative perplexity than the strongest diffusion baselines using far fewer function evaluations (NFE). However, NFE alone does not capture the full inference efficiency picture, since the cost per step differs across different diffusion language models; many DLMs process the full sequence at every step and use samplers that can introduce additional overhead. NCM , on the other hand, processes very few tokens at the coarse levels of its hierarchy, saving compute at these early steps. We benchmark end-to-end wall-clock time for generating 1,024 1{,}024 sequences at batch size 16 16 on a single NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB GPU (Figure 1 ). On LM1B, NCM uses 11 × 11\times fewer NFE than the strongest diffusion language model baseline, DUO, and runs 21 × 21\times faster at better generative perplexity. On XSum, it uses 16 × 16\times fewer NFE than the strongest diffusion baseline, AURORA-LM, and runs 31 × 31\times faster at comparable ROUGE. The speedup gains come from both fewer NFE and a lower average cost per step compared to the DLM baselines. Lower Training Budgets.
